angle: what $100 a month becomes in 20 years, from 3 angles: numbers, psychology, playbook
title: What $100 a Month Becomes in 20 Years

scenes.text: Hi, I'm Ryan Rover. One hundred dollars a month. It's a dinner out for two. A couple of streaming services and a takeout order. It's the kind of money that disappears without anyone noticing. But what if you didn't let it disappear? What if you invested that one hundred dollars every single month for twenty years? Today we're going to find out exactly what it becomes, with real math, and why such a small number can quietly change your life.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Here's the headline. One hundred dollars a month for twenty years, at a seven percent average yearly return, grows to roughly fifty two thousand dollars. You'd put in twenty four thousand. The other twenty eight thousand is growth.
scenes.short_hook: What does one hundred dollars a month become in twenty years?

scenes.text: Let's be honest about what that number means. Fifty two thousand dollars won't make you a millionaire. But it's an emergency fund, a down payment on a home in many parts of the country, a year or two of retirement income, or a debt free start for a child. And it came from money most people spend without noticing. More importantly, one hundred dollars a month is just the beginning. Once you see how the math works, you'll understand why people who start small often end up investing much more.
scenes.caption: $24,000 IN, $52,000 OUT

scenes.text: We'll explore this from three angles. First, the numbers. What one hundred dollars a month becomes at different returns, over different time periods, and after fees, taxes and inflation. Second, the psychology. Why small amounts feel pointless, and why that feeling is so misleading. And third, the playbook. Exactly where to put your one hundred dollars, in what order, so it works as hard as possible. Quick reminder. Seven percent is an illustration, not a promise. Markets go up and down, and real returns will vary.
scenes.caption: THREE ANGLES

scenes.text: Let's start with the numbers. And the first lesson is about the most important ingredient in this whole recipe.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Our numbers. All growth examples use monthly compounding with stated average yearly returns, like four, seven and ten percent. These are illustrations, not predictions. Historical stock market data comes from sources like the S and P Dow Jones Indices, and long run return research from economists like Aswath Damodaran at New York University. Account rules come from the IRS. Inflation data comes from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. This is education, not financial advice.
scenes.caption: OUR NUMBERS

scenes.text: Angle one. The numbers. Seven lessons about what one hundred dollars a month really becomes.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Lesson number one. Time matters more than the amount.
scenes.caption: LESSON 1

scenes.text: Here's what one hundred dollars a month becomes at a seven percent average yearly return, over different lengths of time. After ten years, roughly seventeen thousand dollars. After twenty years, roughly fifty two thousand. After thirty years, roughly one hundred twenty two thousand. After forty years, roughly two hundred sixty two thousand. Notice something. Each extra ten years more than doubles the result.
scenes.caption: 10, 20, 30, 40 YEARS

scenes.text: That's compounding. In the early years, most of your balance is money you put in. In the later years, most of it is growth on growth. By year forty in our example, you've contributed forty eight thousand dollars, and the growth is more than two hundred thousand. Time doesn't just add to the result. It multiplies it.
scenes.caption: GROWTH ON GROWTH

scenes.text: This is why starting early is so powerful. Someone who invests one hundred dollars a month from age twenty five to sixty five could end up with far more than someone who invests two hundred dollars a month from forty five to sixty five, even though the second person puts in the same total amount over a shorter period. Time does the heavy lifting.
scenes.caption: EARLY BEATS BIG

scenes.text: Try this. Open a free compound interest calculator online. Enter one hundred dollars a month, seven percent, and your own number of years until retirement. Look at how much of the final number is growth. That one screen can change how you think about every dollar.
scenes.caption: RUN YOUR NUMBERS

scenes.text: Here's the forty year version. One hundred dollars a month for forty years, at a seven percent average yearly return, grows to roughly two hundred sixty two thousand dollars. Total put in, forty eight thousand.
Lesson number two. The return rate makes a huge difference.
scenes.caption: LESSON 2

scenes.text: Let's try different returns over twenty years. At four percent, one hundred dollars a month becomes roughly thirty seven thousand dollars. At seven percent, roughly fifty two thousand. At ten percent, roughly seventy six thousand. Same contributions. Same time. The only difference is the average return.
scenes.caption: 4% VS 7% VS 10%

scenes.text: Where do those numbers come from? Over very long periods, the US stock market, as measured by the S and P five hundred, has historically returned roughly ten percent a year on average before inflation, according to long run data. After inflation, it's been closer to seven percent. Bonds have historically returned less. A savings account usually returns less still. But past returns are no guarantee of future returns, and some decades have been much worse than average.
scenes.caption: HISTORY, NOT A PROMISE

scenes.text: That's why many people use seven percent for planning. It's a rough estimate of long run stock returns after inflation, so the result is in today's dollars. If you use ten percent, you should remember that the result is in future dollars, which will buy less because of inflation.
scenes.caption: WHY 7% FOR PLANNING

scenes.text: Try this. Run your numbers at four, seven and ten percent. Plan with the middle or lower number, and treat anything better as a bonus. Conservative planning means fewer unpleasant surprises.
scenes.caption: PLAN CONSERVATIVELY

scenes.text: Lesson number three. Fees matter more than you think.
scenes.caption: LESSON 3

scenes.text: Let's say your investment earns seven percent before fees. In a low cost index fund with a fee of a small fraction of a percent, you keep almost all of that. In a fund charging one percent a year, your effective return drops to around six percent. On one hundred dollars a month over twenty years, that's the difference between roughly fifty two thousand dollars and roughly forty six thousand.
scenes.caption: 7% VS 6% AFTER FEES
scenes.short_hook: A tiny fee can eat thousands of your dollars. Here's how.

scenes.text: Over forty years, the gap gets much bigger, because fees compound just like returns. A one percent fee can take a surprisingly large share of your final balance over a lifetime of investing. And the fee is charged every year, whether your investments go up or down.
scenes.caption: FEES COMPOUND TOO

scenes.text: This is a big reason low cost index funds became so popular. Researchers like those at S and P Dow Jones Indices, in their SPIVA reports, have found that over long periods most actively managed funds underperformed their benchmark index after fees. Lower costs are one of the few things investors can fully control.
scenes.caption: COSTS YOU CAN CONTROL

scenes.text: Try this. Look up the expense ratio of every fund you own, in your retirement plan and anywhere else. If you see one percent or more, check whether your plan offers a lower cost alternative in the same category.
scenes.caption: CHECK YOUR FEES

scenes.text: Lesson number four. Inflation means future dollars buy less.
scenes.caption: LESSON 4

scenes.text: Inflation is the gradual rise in prices over time. The Federal Reserve targets about two percent inflation a year over the longer run, and actual inflation has sometimes been much higher, as Americans saw in twenty twenty two. At three percent inflation, prices roughly double in about twenty four years.
scenes.caption: PRICES RISE

scenes.text: That's why the seven percent example is useful. Because it's roughly a return after inflation, fifty two thousand dollars in twenty years means roughly the buying power of fifty two thousand dollars today. If you used a ten percent nominal return, you'd get a bigger number, but it would buy less.
scenes.caption: TODAY'S DOLLARS

scenes.text: Inflation is also why keeping long term money in cash is risky in its own way. A savings account paying less than inflation slowly loses buying power, even though the balance never goes down. For short term money, that's fine. For twenty year money, it's a real cost.
scenes.caption: CASH LOSES BUYING POWER

scenes.text: Try this. When you see any long term projection, ask, is this in today's dollars or future dollars? It's one of the most useful questions in personal finance.
scenes.caption: TODAY'S OR FUTURE DOLLARS?

scenes.text: Lesson number five. The type of account changes what you keep.
scenes.caption: LESSON 5

scenes.text: In a regular taxable brokerage account, you may owe taxes on dividends each year and on gains when you sell. In tax advantaged accounts like a four oh one k or an IRA, the money can grow without yearly taxes. That difference can add up to thousands of dollars over twenty years.
scenes.caption: TAXABLE VS TAX ADVANTAGED

scenes.text: A Roth IRA is especially powerful for small, long term contributions. You contribute money you've already paid tax on, and if you follow the rules, qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax free, including all the growth. On our fifty two thousand dollar example, that could mean all twenty eight thousand of growth is never taxed. Income limits and rules apply, so check the current IRS guidelines.
scenes.caption: TAX FREE GROWTH

scenes.text: A traditional four oh one k or IRA works differently. Contributions may reduce your taxes today, and you pay income tax when you withdraw in retirement. Both can be great choices. The best one depends on your tax bracket now and what you expect it to be later.
scenes.caption: PAY TAX NOW OR LATER

scenes.text: Try this. If you're investing one hundred dollars a month, find out whether you have access to a workplace plan with a match, and whether you're eligible for a Roth IRA. Those are usually the first places to look.
scenes.caption: FIND THE RIGHT ACCOUNT

scenes.text: Lesson number six. Increasing the amount, even slowly, changes everything.
scenes.caption: LESSON 6

scenes.text: One hundred dollars a month for twenty years at seven percent becomes roughly fifty two thousand dollars. Two hundred dollars becomes roughly one hundred four thousand. Five hundred dollars becomes roughly two hundred sixty thousand. The growth scales directly with the amount.

But you don't need to jump straight to five hundred. If you start at one hundred and raise it by just a few percent every year, perhaps when you get a raise, the final result can be dramatically higher than staying at one hundred forever. Small increases compound on top of compounding.
scenes.caption: STEP IT UP

scenes.text: This is where many people's financial lives quietly turn around. They start small, see the balance grow, feel motivated, and gradually increase. Five years later, they're investing several hundred dollars a month, and it feels normal.
scenes.caption: SMALL STARTS GROW

scenes.text: Try this. Set a calendar reminder for every raise or every new year, to increase your monthly investment by at least ten dollars. You'll barely notice the difference in your budget, but your future self will.
scenes.caption: PLUS TEN DOLLARS

scenes.text: Here's what five hundred dollars a month becomes over twenty years at a seven percent average yearly return. Roughly two hundred sixty thousand dollars. Total put in, one hundred twenty thousand.
Lesson number seven. The path won't be smooth.

card.title: Bad years are part of it

scenes.caption: LESSON 7
scenes.chapter: 7. Bad years are part of it

scenes.text: Seven percent is an average. In real life, some years will be much better and some much worse. The US stock market fell about thirty seven percent in two thousand eight, including dividends, and about eighteen percent in twenty twenty two, according to S and P five hundred total return data. There will be years when your one hundred dollars a month seems to be shrinking.
scenes.caption: -37% IN 2008

scenes.text: But here's the twist. When you invest the same amount every month, bad years mean you buy more shares at lower prices. That's called dollar cost averaging. It doesn't guarantee profits or prevent losses, but it means market drops aren't only bad news. They're also a sale on what you're buying.
scenes.caption: BUYING ON SALE

scenes.text: Historically, investors who kept investing through downturns were generally better off than those who stopped or sold in a panic. The biggest risk for a small monthly investor often isn't the market. It's quitting.
scenes.caption: DON'T QUIT

scenes.text: Try this. Write a one sentence note to your future self today. When the market drops, I will keep investing my one hundred dollars a month. Put it where you'll see it.
scenes.caption: A NOTE TO FUTURE YOU

scenes.text: That's angle one. Time, return rate, fees, inflation, taxes, raising the amount, and the bumpy path. Now angle two. The psychology. Because the math is simple. The hard part is actually doing it, month after month.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: If the math is so clear, why doesn't everyone invest one hundred dollars a month? Because our brains aren't built for long term compounding. We think in straight lines, we value today over tomorrow, and small amounts feel pointless. Let's look at the mental hurdles, and how to jump over them.
scenes.caption: THE MENTAL HURDLES

scenes.text: Lesson number eight. One hundred dollars feels too small to bother.

card.title: It feels too small to matter

scenes.caption: LESSON 8
scenes.chapter: 8. It feels too small to matter

scenes.text: Many people think, what's the point of investing one hundred dollars? I'll start when I can invest real money. But waiting costs time, and time is the most valuable ingredient. Five years of waiting can mean losing a large share of the final result.
scenes.caption: WHY BOTHER?
scenes.short_hook: One hundred dollars feels too small to matter. It isn't.

scenes.text: Economists Victor Stango and Jonathan Zinman described exponential growth bias, our tendency to underestimate compounding. We imagine growth as a straight line, so small amounts look small forever. In reality, they curve upward over time.
scenes.caption: STRAIGHT LINE THINKING

scenes.text: There's also a habit benefit. Investing one hundred dollars teaches you how accounts work, how markets move, and how it feels to see a drop. When you have more money later, you'll already know what to do.
scenes.caption: PRACTICE WITH SMALL MONEY

scenes.text: Try this. Instead of asking whether one hundred dollars matters, ask what it becomes in twenty or thirty years. Then start this month.
scenes.caption: START THIS MONTH

scenes.text: Lesson number nine. There's no perfect time to start.
scenes.caption: LESSON 9

scenes.text: People often wait for the market to drop, or for things to calm down, before investing. But nobody can reliably predict short term market moves. Missing even a handful of the best days in the market historically reduced long term returns significantly, according to analyses by firms like J.P. Morgan Asset Management.
scenes.caption: TIMING THE MARKET

scenes.text: Many of the best days happened close to the worst days, during periods of high fear. Investors who sat out to avoid the bad days often missed the recovery too. In other words, the moments that feel most dangerous are often the moments when staying invested matters most.
scenes.caption: BEST DAYS NEAR WORST DAYS

scenes.text: For a monthly investor, the solution is simple. Invest the same amount on the same day every month, regardless of headlines. That removes the timing decision entirely.
scenes.caption: SAME DAY EVERY MONTH

scenes.text: Try this. Pick a date right after payday and set your automatic investment for that day. Then stop checking the news to decide.
scenes.caption: AUTOMATE THE DATE

scenes.text: Lesson number ten. Today always feels more important than twenty years from now.

card.title: Present bias
card.sub: the latte today vs the money later

scenes.caption: LESSON 10

scenes.text: Present bias makes immediate rewards feel much bigger than future ones. One hundred dollars today feels like a nice dinner. Fifty two thousand dollars in twenty years feels abstract.
scenes.caption: TODAY FEELS BIGGER

scenes.text: Some research has found that when people see age progressed images of themselves, they become more willing to save for the future. Making the future feel real helps fight present bias.
scenes.caption: MEET FUTURE YOU

scenes.text: Another trick is to tie the future money to something specific. Not just retirement, but freedom to change careers, a paid off house, or helping your kids. Specific goals feel more real.
scenes.caption: MAKE IT SPECIFIC

scenes.text: Try this. Give your investment account a nickname, like freedom fund or future house. It sounds small, but naming your goal can make it feel closer.
scenes.caption: NAME YOUR GOAL

scenes.text: Lesson number eleven. Checking your account too often can make you a worse investor.
scenes.caption: LESSON 11

scenes.text: Markets go up and down daily. If you check every day, you'll see a lot of red. Research on loss aversion shows losses feel about twice as painful as equal gains feel good. Frequent checking magnifies the pain.
scenes.caption: DAILY RED

scenes.text: Studies by Shlomo Benartzi and Richard Thaler described myopic loss aversion. Investors who looked at results more often tended to take less risk and choose worse long term strategies.
scenes.caption: MYOPIC LOSS AVERSION

scenes.text: For a twenty year plan, checking once a month or even once a quarter is plenty. You'll see the long term trend instead of the daily noise.
scenes.caption: CHECK QUARTERLY

scenes.text: Try this. Delete the investing app from your home screen, or turn off price notifications. Let the money work while you live your life.
scenes.caption: TURN OFF THE NOISE

scenes.text: Quick break. If this is helping you see small money differently, subscribe to Ryan Rover Money. It's free and it helps the channel grow. Okay, lesson twelve.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Lesson number twelve. Don't compare your hundred dollars with someone else's thousands.
scenes.caption: LESSON 12

scenes.text: Online, you'll see people investing thousands a month, or showing huge gains. That can make one hundred dollars feel embarrassing. But comparison is a trap. You don't know their income, their debt, or their losses.
scenes.caption: THE COMPARISON TRAP

scenes.text: Every investor starts somewhere. Many people who invest large amounts today started with small automatic contributions years ago. The difference is that they kept going.
scenes.caption: EVERYONE STARTS SMALL

scenes.text: Your plan only has to work for you. One hundred dollars a month, kept up for decades and increased over time, is a real plan.
scenes.caption: YOUR OWN PLAN

scenes.text: Try this. Track only your own progress. Write down your balance every six months and compare it with your past self.
scenes.caption: COMPARE WITH YOUR PAST

scenes.text: Lesson number thirteen. Fear of losing money keeps many people from starting.
scenes.caption: LESSON 13

scenes.text: Investing does involve risk. Stock prices can fall, sometimes a lot. But not investing has its own risk. Inflation slowly erodes cash, and missing decades of growth can leave you short in retirement.
scenes.caption: FEAR OF LOSING

scenes.text: Diversification reduces the risk of any single company failing. Broad index funds hold hundreds or thousands of companies. A long time horizon gives investments time to recover from downturns. Historically, the longer the holding period, the less often broad US stock investments ended with a loss, though there are no guarantees and some long periods have been disappointing.
scenes.caption: SPREAD THE RISK

scenes.text: Your emergency fund also helps. If you have cash for surprises, you won't be forced to sell investments at a bad time.
scenes.caption: CASH FOR SURPRISES

scenes.text: Try this. Before investing, build a small emergency fund. Then invest money you won't need for at least five years.
scenes.caption: EMERGENCY FUND FIRST

scenes.text: Lesson number fourteen. Motivation fades, so systems matter.
scenes.caption: LESSON 14

scenes.text: Starting is exciting. Month thirty seven is boring. Many people stop contributing after the novelty wears off, or when life gets busy. A move, a new baby, a job change, and suddenly the transfer gets paused and never restarted. Those pauses, more than market crashes, are what quietly shrink many people's results.
scenes.caption: MONTH 37 IS BORING

scenes.text: That's why automation matters so much. Once the transfer is automatic, it happens whether you feel motivated or not. Research on automatic enrollment in retirement plans shows defaults have a huge effect on participation.
scenes.caption: AUTOMATION WINS

scenes.text: Visual reminders help too. A chart of your balance on the fridge, or a yearly check in where you celebrate progress.
scenes.caption: CELEBRATE PROGRESS

scenes.text: Try this. Once a year, on the same date, check your balance, celebrate your progress, and raise your contribution.
scenes.caption: ONCE A YEAR

scenes.text: That's angle two. Small numbers, timing, present bias, checking too often, comparison, fear and fading motivation. Now angle three. The playbook. Exactly where to put your one hundred dollars, in order.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Here's the practical part. If you have one hundred dollars a month to invest, where should it go first? Many financial planners suggest a similar order. It's not the only approach, but it's a solid starting point for most people.
scenes.caption: THE ORDER

scenes.text: Step one. Build a small emergency fund first.
scenes.caption: LESSON 15

scenes.text: Before investing, many planners suggest saving at least a starter emergency fund, often around one thousand dollars, in a high yield savings account. This keeps surprises from landing on a credit card.
scenes.caption: $1,000 FIRST

scenes.text: If you invest without a cushion, a car repair could force you to sell investments, possibly at a loss. Or worse, it could land on a credit card at over twenty percent interest, wiping out years of investment gains in a few months. The emergency fund protects the investing plan.
scenes.caption: AVOID FORCED SALES

scenes.text: High yield savings accounts insured by the FDIC have offered much better rates than traditional savings accounts in recent years. Your emergency money stays safe and easy to reach, and it still earns something while it waits. Over time, many planners suggest growing it to three to six months of essential expenses.
scenes.caption: FDIC INSURED

scenes.text: Try this. Send your first months of one hundred dollars to a separate savings account until you hit one thousand.
scenes.caption: THEN INVEST

scenes.text: Step two. Pay off high interest debt.

card.title: Step 2: Pay off high interest debt

scenes.caption: LESSON 16
scenes.chapter: 16. Step 2: Pay off high interest debt

scenes.text: If you carry credit card debt at twenty percent or more, paying it off is like earning a guaranteed twenty percent return. That beats the long run average of the stock market.
scenes.caption: A GUARANTEED RETURN

scenes.text: One hundred dollars a month extra toward a card balance can shorten payoff by years and save hundreds or thousands in interest. And unlike the stock market, that return is certain. Every dollar of high interest debt you pay off is a dollar that stops working against you.
scenes.caption: YEARS FASTER

scenes.text: Once the debt is gone, redirect the same one hundred dollars, plus the old minimum payment, into investing.
scenes.caption: REDIRECT IT

scenes.text: Try this. List debts by interest rate. Attack the highest rate first.
scenes.caption: HIGHEST RATE FIRST

scenes.text: Step three. Get your full employer match.
scenes.caption: LESSON 17

scenes.text: If your employer matches part of your retirement contributions, that's an instant return. A fifty percent match turns one hundred dollars into one hundred fifty, before any market growth.
scenes.caption: $100 BECOMES $150
scenes.short_hook: If your job offers this, you're leaving free money on the table.

scenes.text: With a match, one hundred dollars a month could grow much faster than our example, because the employer is adding money too. With a fifty percent match, the same twenty years at seven percent could produce roughly seventy eight thousand dollars instead of fifty two thousand, and you'd still have contributed only twenty four thousand of your own money.
scenes.caption: FASTER GROWTH

scenes.text: Check your plan's vesting schedule, which determines when the matched money fully belongs to you. Some employers vest immediately, while others require a few years of service. Knowing the schedule helps you make smarter decisions if you're thinking about changing jobs.
scenes.caption: CHECK VESTING

scenes.text: Try this. Find out your match formula and contribute at least enough to get all of it.
scenes.caption: GET THE FULL MATCH

scenes.text: Step four. Consider a Roth IRA.
scenes.caption: LESSON 18

scenes.text: After the match, many people open a Roth IRA, if they're eligible based on income. You can invest small amounts, and qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax free.
scenes.caption: TAX FREE LATER

scenes.text: Many brokerages let you open an IRA with no minimum and buy fractional shares of index funds, so one hundred dollars a month works perfectly. You can set up a recurring transfer and a recurring investment in a few minutes, and from then on it runs on its own.
scenes.caption: NO MINIMUMS

scenes.text: Roth contributions, but not earnings, can generally be withdrawn without penalty, which gives some flexibility. Rules are detailed, so check IRS guidance.
scenes.caption: KNOW THE RULES

scenes.text: Try this. Compare a few low cost brokerages and open a Roth IRA if you qualify.
scenes.caption: OPEN ONE

scenes.text: Step five. Choose simple, low cost, diversified investments.
scenes.caption: LESSON 19

scenes.text: For many people, a broad stock market index fund or a target date fund is a simple choice. A target date fund automatically adjusts the mix of stocks and bonds as you approach retirement.
scenes.caption: SIMPLE CHOICES

scenes.text: Avoid chasing hot stocks or trends with your core money. Simple, diversified and low cost tends to win over long periods. If you want to experiment with individual stocks for fun or learning, many people limit it to a small share of their investments, money they can afford to lose, while the core stays in broad funds.
scenes.caption: SKIP THE HYPE

scenes.text: Check the expense ratio before you buy. Lower is usually better.
scenes.caption: LOW COST

scenes.text: Try this. Pick one broad, low cost fund and stick with it. Simplicity helps you stay consistent.
scenes.caption: PICK ONE

scenes.text: Step six. Automate, then increase.
scenes.caption: LESSON 20

scenes.text: Set your one hundred dollars to invest automatically every month. Then increase it whenever you can, especially after raises or when debts are paid off.
scenes.caption: AUTOMATE

scenes.text: Many workplace plans offer automatic yearly increases. Turning that on can raise your savings without any effort.
scenes.caption: AUTO INCREASE

scenes.text: Over time, one hundred dollars can become two hundred, then five hundred. The habit you build with one hundred dollars is what makes that possible. Most people who invest large amounts today didn't start large. They started with an amount that felt manageable, and kept nudging it upward year after year.
scenes.caption: $100 TO $500

scenes.text: Try this. Set your automatic investment today, and set a reminder to raise it in six months.
scenes.caption: START TODAY

scenes.text: Now, you might be thinking, I don't have an extra one hundred dollars. Let's find it. Here are ten common places it hides in a typical budget.
scenes.caption: RYAN
scenes.chapter: Where to find one hundred dollars a month

scenes.text: One. Subscriptions you don't use. Many households have two or three forgotten ones, easily twenty to forty dollars a month. Two. Bank fees. Switching to a no fee account can save monthly maintenance and overdraft charges. Three. Your phone plan. Many people pay for far more data than they use, and switching to a cheaper plan or carrier can save twenty dollars or more a month.
scenes.caption: PLACES 1 TO 3

scenes.text: Four. Insurance. Shopping your car and home insurance once a year can lower your premium. Five. Takeout and delivery. Replacing just two delivery meals a month with home cooking can free up forty or fifty dollars. Six. Grocery waste. Planning meals and using what you buy can cut spending noticeably. Seven. Brand names. Switching ten regular items to store brands can save real money with no real difference.
scenes.caption: PLACES 4 TO 7

scenes.text: Eight. Your tax refund. If you get a big refund every year, adjusting your withholding can add money to every paycheck, money you could invest monthly instead of waiting a year. Nine. Selling things you don't use. A one time sale can fund several months of investing. And ten. Your next raise. Commit now to investing part of it before you ever get used to spending it.
scenes.caption: PLACES 8 TO 10

scenes.text: You don't need all ten. Most people can find one hundred dollars with just three or four of these. The important thing is to move the money automatically as soon as you find it, so it doesn't quietly get absorbed into other spending.
scenes.caption: MOVE IT AS SOON AS YOU FIND IT

scenes.text: Here's what one hundred dollars a month, at a seven percent average yearly return, could become by age sixty five, depending on when you start. Start at twenty, and it could be roughly three hundred eighty thousand dollars. Start at thirty, roughly one hundred eighty thousand. Start at forty, roughly eighty one thousand. Start at fifty, roughly thirty two thousand.
scenes.caption: START AT 20, 30, 40 OR 50
scenes.chapter: One hundred dollars a month at every age

scenes.text: Look at the gap between twenty and thirty. Ten years of one hundred dollars, just twelve thousand dollars of contributions, makes a difference of about two hundred thousand dollars by sixty five. That's the price of waiting a decade. It's the most expensive decision many people never realize they made.
scenes.caption: THE COST OF WAITING

scenes.text: If you're older, don't be discouraged. The lesson is the same. Start now, and invest more than one hundred dollars if you can, because you have fewer years for compounding. Many people in their forties and fifties are in their highest earning years, and catch up contribution rules for people fifty and older allow them to put more into retirement accounts.
scenes.caption: IF YOU'RE STARTING LATER

scenes.text: Mistake one. Stopping during a market drop. That's when your one hundred dollars buys the most shares. Mistake two. Picking expensive funds. A high fee on a small balance still compounds against you for decades. Mistake three. Cashing out early. Withdrawing from retirement accounts early can mean taxes and penalties, and it resets the compounding clock.
scenes.caption: MISTAKES 1 TO 3

scenes.text: Mistake four. Chasing hot tips with your monthly money. Small amounts are easy to gamble with, and that's exactly why it's tempting. Keep your core plan boring. Mistake five. Never increasing the amount. One hundred dollars is a wonderful start, but the people who end up with the most are the ones who raise it whenever they can.
scenes.caption: MISTAKES 4 AND 5

scenes.text: So what can roughly fifty two thousand dollars actually do for you in twenty years? Option one. It can be the backbone of your safety net. With that much invested, a job loss or a medical bill becomes a setback, not a crisis. That kind of security changes how you negotiate at work, how you sleep at night, and how much risk you can take with your career.
scenes.caption: A SAFETY NET
scenes.chapter: What fifty two thousand dollars can do

scenes.text: Option two. It can keep growing. If you stop contributing at year twenty and simply leave the fifty two thousand invested at the same seven percent average return, it could roughly double again in about ten years, by the rule of seventy two. Your one hundred dollars a month keeps working long after you stop paying in.
scenes.caption: IT KEEPS GROWING

scenes.text: Option three. It can produce income. Using the four percent guideline many retirement planners mention, fifty two thousand dollars could support roughly two thousand dollars of withdrawals a year. That's not a full income, but it's a meaningful supplement, and it came from money most people never noticed spending.
scenes.caption: A LITTLE INCOME

scenes.text: And option four, the most important one. It can prove to you that this works. Once you've watched one hundred dollars a month turn into tens of thousands, you'll never look at small money the same way again. That belief is often worth more than the money itself.
scenes.caption: PROOF IT WORKS

scenes.text: Let me show you how this plays out with three people.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Alex starts investing one hundred dollars a month at twenty five and never increases it. At sixty five, at a seven percent average yearly return, that could grow to roughly two hundred sixty thousand dollars. Not bad for money that felt too small to matter.
scenes.caption: ALEX: $100 FROM 25
scenes.short_hook: Waiting ten years can cut your result in half.

scenes.text: Jamie waits until thirty five to start, also with one hundred dollars a month. At sixty five, that could be roughly one hundred twenty two thousand dollars. Waiting ten years cut the result by more than half.
scenes.caption: JAMIE: STARTS AT 35

scenes.text: Morgan starts at twenty five with one hundred dollars a month, and increases the contribution a little every year. By the end, Morgan could have far more than both of them. Same starting amount. The difference was starting early and growing the habit.
scenes.caption: MORGAN: STARTS AND GROWS

scenes.text: Question one. Is one hundred dollars a month really worth it? Yes. It builds the habit, gets compounding started and grows into a meaningful amount over decades. And it usually becomes more than one hundred dollars as your income grows.
scenes.caption: IS IT WORTH IT?

scenes.text: Question two. What if I can only invest fifty dollars? Start with fifty. Many brokerages allow small amounts and fractional shares. The habit matters more than the amount.
scenes.caption: WHAT ABOUT $50?

scenes.text: Question three. What if the market crashes right after I start? Then you're buying at lower prices. For a twenty year plan, early drops can actually help, as long as you keep investing.
scenes.caption: WHAT IF IT CRASHES?

scenes.text: Question four. Should I invest or pay off my student loans? It depends on the interest rate. High interest debt usually comes first. For low interest debt, many people do both, especially to get an employer match.
scenes.caption: LOANS OR INVEST?

scenes.text: Question five. Should I invest my one hundred dollars all at once each year, or monthly? Research on lump sum versus monthly investing suggests that investing sooner has historically done better more often, because markets have tended to rise over time. But for most people, money arrives monthly with each paycheck, so investing monthly is the natural and practical choice. The important thing is that it happens consistently.
scenes.caption: MONTHLY OR YEARLY?

scenes.text: Question six. Can I lose all my money? With a single stock, yes, a company can fail. With a broad index fund holding hundreds or thousands of companies, losing everything would require nearly the entire market to collapse permanently. Values can still drop sharply for a time, which is why money you need soon shouldn't be in stocks.
scenes.caption: CAN I LOSE IT ALL?

scenes.text: Quick recap. Angle one, the numbers. Time is the main ingredient, the rate changes everything, fees eat growth, inflation shrinks the number, the right account matters, raising the amount changes everything, and bad years are part of it.
scenes.caption: THE NUMBERS: 1 TO 7

scenes.text: Angle two, the psychology. It feels too small, there's no perfect time, present bias, checking too often, comparing, fear of losing, and fading motivation.
scenes.caption: THE PSYCHOLOGY: 8 TO 14

scenes.text: Angle three, the playbook. Emergency fund, high interest debt, employer match, Roth IRA, simple low cost funds, and automate and increase.
scenes.caption: THE PLAYBOOK: 15 TO 20

scenes.text: One hundred dollars a month won't change your life this month. But in twenty years, it can change everything. Set it up today. If you want the full plan, it's in my playbook, linked in the description. Tell me in the comments how many years you have to invest. I'm Ryan Rover. See you in the next one.
scenes.caption: RYAN
